title: a reassigned binding and a conditional layer stay opaque when a type-only wrapper is put around them, rather than being read through the wrapper's type
notes: specification/requirements.mdx, 'Satisfaction': 'When the compiler knows the complete closure, an unsatisfied capability MUST be a compile error.' The compiler does NOT know the closure in either statement here, and `SMITHERS2104` is the honest answer for that: a `let` that is reassigned to a different layer after its initializer, and a `?:` whose branches provide different capabilities, are both expressions whose provided set is not statically one set. Wrapping either in `satisfies Layer<typeof Directory> | Layer<typeof Clock>` does not change that; it only writes down a type that is true of both branches and names neither. WHY THIS CASE EXISTS: it is the other side of the wrapper-stripping fix landed on 2026-08-27. That fix has to see THROUGH a wrapper — `a-layer-through-a-type-only-wrapper-is-the-same-layer` requires it — and the failure mode of any such fix is that it strips the wrapper and then believes whatever it finds, or that it stops at the wrapper and reads the wrapper's TYPE instead of its operand. Both of those turn these two statements green: the declared union type is satisfiable, and `swapped`'s initializer alone provides Directory. Neither is a statement about what the program does. The `let` statement is deliberately reassigned to a Clock layer and then provided to a body requiring Directory, and the conditional's first branch is the Directory one, so a resolver that follows the initializer, or that takes the first branch, produces a program that compiles and panics rather than one that merely mis-diagnoses. WHY TWO STATEMENTS IN ONE CASE: they are two spellings of one obligation and they fail together under every fix that would break either — the shared cause is 'the wrapper's type is not the operand's provided set'. Splitting them would double the file count without doubling the evidence. They print at different lines and columns, so the expectation still tells them apart and a fix that closes one and opens the other is visible. WHAT THIS CASE DELIBERATELY DOES NOT PIN: the message. `SMITHERS2104` carries a fixed sentence with no payload — the two backends word it differently ('this POC cannot prove' versus 'the compiler cannot prove') and neither names a capability, a branch, or a binding — so `messageContains` would add no promise and would freeze wording that is explicitly not the contract. It also does not pin `SMITHERS2101`: an opaque layer contributes no known provided set, so there is no capability to report as unsatisfied, and declaring one would ratify a cascade neither backend produces. VERIFIED LOAD-BEARING, not assumed: mutating the SECOND declared line from 30 to 28 — which makes the expectation two diagnostics at one position, the shape a backend that reported both statements at the first one would produce — turns the case red on BOTH backends with the position diff printed, and the file was restored byte-identically (sha256 9d0a521d6c52d326329e7a1d893a44214873ff469c833603665327e16a17f8c2 before and after, that digest being this file's content at the moment the mutation ran — the sentence recording it is appended afterwards, so the shipped file necessarily hashes differently). The paired positive control is `a-layer-through-a-type-only-wrapper-is-the-same-layer`, which wraps a `const` initializer in the same `satisfies` and must keep compiling AND RUNNING, so a fix that answers `SMITHERS2104` for every wrapped layer turns that case red instead of passing this one for the wrong reason.
